title: A Cordial Intro Email to Boston
subtitle: The logical follow-up to "A Love Letter to Madison"
html:
Preface: A simple ask—please don’t mistake my observations for judgements. This post is primarily about things I’ve noticed, not my judgements of them.

Hi Boston,

Like every other milestone in life, my move here revealed that, no matter where I am or what I’m doing, I’m still me. And, as a puppy does, my strengths, weaknesses, and uncanny tendency to attract people with mental illnesses1 follow me around wherever I go. Truly, I don’t know how they find me.

My friend* hypothesized, “It’s the golden retriever energy. You just radiate a gold mist in a 500-mile radius.” I’m not sure if she’s right, but there does seem to be something about how I exist in the world that encourages certain flavors of people to take refuge in my company.2 And, honestly, I’m still trying to figure out what to make of that.

In my very first weekend in town, I stumbled upon a music hangout in Cambridge where a bunch of musicians were playing random songs and jamming to their hearts’ content. An old man asked me if I played, to which I sheepishly replied that I play guitar and piano. The old man then handed me his guitar, which he swapped out for his mandolin. Moments after I sat down and started jamming, a beautiful young woman sat down next to me and said something like, “Hey, I’m Mack3. I have memory problems.”

After a single, clumsy date, Mack and I decided on the friend route. She seemed a good enough person and a good enough musician. That seemed reason enough not to burn any bridges. Now, the more I get to know Mack, the more I get the sense that she came for the biceps (I was wearing a wifebeater at the jam), but stayed (as friends) for the golden retriever energy and safety. Maybe my friend* had a point.

Mack does, in fact, have memory problems… and cancer… and bipolar disorder. She’s a bit of a mess (I say that with love), but she is also one of the bravest people I’ve ever met. And man, she’s a great songwriter. Most of our interactions are music-related, but a non-trivial proportion of them are variations of me letting her know that it’s okay that she’s struggling and that I like her anyway.

“Char, why are you my friend?” is a regularly asked question—one soaked in pain and mistrust.

I remind her every time, but, as you now know, she has memory problems. She’ll ask again soon.

I think having these kinds of conversations—reminding someone that it’s okay not to be okay, and meaning it—is a lost art of sorts. It’s easy to think that people dealt hands much worse than our own are somehow flawed or broken, or that they aren’t worthy of compassion and grace. But that perspective is rooted in a misunderstanding of human nature. Nobody makes themselves. Nobody chooses to be sick.

To be someone people know will offer them a shoulder to cry on, or some ears to listen, feels like a burden and a privilege sometimes. And I’m still trying to figure out how to carry the burden well. It’s easy to slough it off and push away those who are hurting. And it’s almost as easy to stop everything you’re doing and pour all of your energy into helping them. That’s codependency and a savior complex in a nutshell. Both options are bad. The fine line that needs walking—and the one I’m learning to walk—is one where you maintain boundaries that are impermeable enough to others’ problems so that they do not become yours, but permeable enough to them so that you can understand, empathize with, and, if appropriate, aid in solving them.

Boston, you’re testing me. I haven’t gotten good sleep since I moved here, and the number of underwhelming dates I’ve been on is now in the double digits. Do women in Boston laugh? Asking for a friend. But I am learning—learning about myself; about people; about relationships. Also, I just signed a year-long lease here, so we’ll be spending lots of time together in the coming months. Committing to you is a bit scary considering I don’t have long-term employment plans yet. But I’ll be fine. I’m pretty robust.

I also hope I’ll get to keep making music with Mack and others. Music is one of the few things that make me feel… well, anything, really. Here’s a little sample of what we’ve been cooking up. It’s called 🐞.

This post includes audio — listen on Substack.

And if it’s not too much to ask, can you keep the AQI below 100, please?

That’d be great, thanks.

Cheers,

Charlie

1

“mental illnesses” used in a morally neutral, judgement-free way.

2

I might be giving myself too much credit, though. And I’m in no way intending to sound grandiose. I’m just recognizing patterns.

3

Name changed for privacy.
